Dinah
DYE-nuh
proper noun (Old Testament figure)
Dinah (Hebrew Dinah) means "judgment" or "vindicated," from the root for judging; she was the daughter of Jacob by Leah.

See also: Dinah

📖 Biblical Definition

Dinah, the daughter of Jacob and Leah, is the central figure of the grievous history in Genesis 34. When she went out to see the daughters of the land, Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, took her, and defiled her, humbling her by force. Though his soul afterward clave to the maiden and he sought her in marriage, the wrong against the covenant household could not be undone. The narrative is a true and sober account of the corruption of the Canaanite nations and the perils that beset Israel when she mingles with the heathen. Jacob's sons Simeon and Levi, full brothers of Dinah, answered the defilement with treachery and slaughter, persuading the men of Shechem to be circumcised and then, while they were sore, falling upon the city and putting every male to the sword. Their deceitful cruelty Jacob rebuked, and on his deathbed he cursed their fierce anger, scattering them in Israel. The account holds forth at once the seriousness of sexual sin against the covenant people, the danger of unequal communion with the wicked, and the evil of avenging wrong by treachery and bloodshed. It teaches that vengeance belongs to the LORD, and that even within the chosen family sin abounds, awaiting the grace that would redeem.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The daughter of Jacob and Leah, defiled at Shechem, whose dishonor provoked the bloody and treacherous vengeance of her brothers.

expand to see more

DINAH, proper noun. From the Hebrew for "judgment" or "vindication"; the daughter of Jacob by Leah.

The maiden whose defilement at Shechem is recorded in Genesis chapter thirty-four.

The occasion of Simeon and Levi's deceitful slaughter of the men of the city.

As it is written, "And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land" (Gen 34:1).

A warning against mingling with the heathen and against avenging wrong by treachery.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 34:1 — "And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land."

Gen 34:2 — "And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her."

Gen 34:25 — "And it came to pass on the third day, when they were sore, that two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brethren, took each man his sword, and came upon the city boldly, and slew all the males."

Gen 49:7 — "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Some modern treatments romanticize Shechem's assault as a love story or recast the chapter chiefly through the lens of grievance, obscuring its moral lessons.

expand to see more

Attempts to soften the chapter into a tale of star-crossed love between Dinah and Shechem run against the plain word that he took her and defiled her by force; Scripture names it a folly wrought in Israel. Equally, readings that reduce the account to a single theme of victimhood eclipse the layered judgment the text renders upon every party—upon Shechem's sin, upon Jacob's passivity and worldly compromise, and upon the murderous treachery of Simeon and Levi, which the dying patriarch cursed.

The principle to recover is the holiness God requires of His covenant people and the evil of repaying wrong with greater wrong. The defilement was a real and grievous sin, and the brothers' vengeance was itself sin, deceitful and bloody. Vengeance belongs to the LORD, who alone judges righteously. The chapter calls Israel out from communion with the corrupt nations and casts every reader upon the need of redeeming grace, since sin festers even in the household of the promise.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The episode is rooted in the danger of Israel's mingling with Canaan and in the seriousness of sin within the covenant family.

expand to see more

Dinah was born to Jacob by Leah, listed among his children (Gen 30:21).

Her going out to see the daughters of the land exposed her to the heathen city.

Shechem's defilement provoked the deceitful covenant of circumcision (Gen 34:13-17).

Simeon and Levi's slaughter brought guilt and danger upon Jacob's house (Gen 34:30).

The deathbed prophecy cursed their cruelty and scattered them in Israel (Gen 49:7).

Usage

"The chapter is cited as a warning against unequal communion with the ungodly."

"Simeon and Levi's deceit is the classic example of vengeance overstepping justice."

"Jacob's rebuke is invoked to show the peril of compromise with surrounding nations."
